note: The Browser Company's 41-second launch spot for Arc for iPhone, cut almost entirely from other people's films. Lonely laptops at night, a snail, Mr. Bean packing a suitcase, the Little Miss Sunshine van, the flying house from Up and the footbridge race from Jules and Jim carry one sentence written in white serif across black cards and live footage: 'Home. What if you could bring home with you? You can. Your home on the internet is now in your pocket.' The app itself gets about seven seconds. The breakdown follows how borrowed footage can carry a product's idea, how one sentence is spread across a montage, and samples 10 moves as flip books.
transcript_kind: Local speech recognition on the separated voice track. Only the two spoken lines lifted from film clips are kept; from 0:19 a song with a sung vocal plays, and its lyrics could not be made out reliably, so they are left out (repeated 'Where's my phone?' cues over it were hallucinations and were removed). The on-screen sentence is laid out in the Craft map

shot_notes.0: Cold open on a found photo-like shot: a white laptop on a cluttered desk with a pizza slice, a water bottle and a plant, lit by a harsh flash. The internet as a place people live in, slightly squalid.
shot_notes.1: 'Home' dissolves on in a white serif over the laptop, centered. The film's one-word thesis arrives before any product does.
shot_notes.2: Hard cut to near black: a face lit only by a laptop screen. 'Home' stays exactly where it was across the cut, so the word reads as a title card and the clips change beneath it.
shot_notes.3: Still dark: the word holds over its second clip. Two very different laptops, one idea.
shot_notes.4: Someone asleep with their head on the desk, then a man alone at a laptop in an empty office. Three short clips of people stuck to their screens.
shot_notes.5: A woman in a bright, washed-out room lifts her laptop over her head as if peering out of it. 'What's out there?' is heard, a line lifted from the clip.
shot_notes.6: A hand reaching across a dark table for something that is not there.
shot_notes.7: A man in black and white looks around an empty room, and 'What' then 'What if' appear word by word. 'Where's my phone?' is heard and the music jumps to full level.
shot_notes.8: Hard cut to color: a teal backpack seen from above, hands grabbing it. Packing begins.
shot_notes.9: A child pulling things out of a lit cupboard, seen from behind.
shot_notes.10: 'you could bring home with you' sits in the middle of a blurry shot of a drawer being emptied in a hurry. The sentence carries over the cut.
shot_notes.11: A white sleeve sweeps clothes out of the drawer. The caption is written smaller than 'Home' and sits across the action, like a subtitle.
shot_notes.12: A snail crossing a path, shallow focus, the clearest picture of the idea: an animal that carries its home on its back. The caption leaves just after the cut to it.
shot_notes.13: Mr. Bean stuffs a suitcase on his bed, letterboxed in a 4:3 frame on black. Archive formats are kept as found rather than cropped to fill.
shot_notes.14: A dim hallway, someone rushing past with bags. The montage is now all leaving.
shot_notes.15: A woman pitches a tent among Joshua trees: a home you can take apart and carry.
shot_notes.16: A family charges down a staircase with luggage, then a woman in a sunhat stuffs a bag into a convertible.
shot_notes.17: The Little Miss Sunshine family pushes the yellow van and jumps in as it rolls.
shot_notes.18: A bus piled high with luggage barrels up a dusty road toward camera. The shots have moved from rooms to roads.
shot_notes.19: Up: children and a mother watch through a window as the balloon house drifts past, reflected in the glass. The song's vocal starts here.
shot_notes.20: The house crosses the reflection; the camera holds on the watchers rather than the house.
shot_notes.21: A father in a striped shirt steps in from the right, looking up. Nobody says anything.
shot_notes.22: The family turns to each other, amazed. The house has become the image of the whole film: a home that travels.
shot_notes.23: 'You can' alone on black, in the same serif. The answer to 'What if' is two words long.
shot_notes.24: A man rides a bicycle down a black-and-white street, pillarboxed. 'You can' is followed by someone simply going.
shot_notes.25: First product frame: Arc's onboarding screen, a white smiley over a purple gradient with 'Hi there'. The smiley blinks once.
shot_notes.26: 'Let's go' button under a small Arc logo on the same gradient, the app's own copy used as a line in the film.
shot_notes.27: Jules and Jim: three friends racing across an iron footbridge, laughing. The film answers the app's 'Let's go' with someone running.
shot_notes.28: The phone UI floats small in the middle of black: a purple space called 'Browser co' with pinned items, then a swipe to a pink 'Crafting' space.
shot_notes.29: 'Your home on the internet' on black, between two spaces.
shot_notes.30: The swipe continues to a yellow 'Home' space with 'Reads for later', 'Home buys', 'Mood board' and 'June trip'. The space is literally named Home.
shot_notes.31: The Home list scrolls, and 'Murakami's vinyl collection' is dragged into place. Personal, specific item names do the warmth.
shot_notes.32: 'is now in your pocket' on black, the end of the sentence.
shot_notes.33: The same caption over a black-and-white hot-air balloon from below, the basket swinging under it.
shot_notes.34: A balloon drifting away in a grey sky behind a tree, the caption still on.
shot_notes.35: An iPhone home screen, Arc's icon between Spotify and Messages, flicking through its alternate icons.
shot_notes.36: The icon keeps changing: candy, pretzel, dark blue, classic. The swap is the app's alternate-icon feature, shown as a flicker.
shot_notes.37: Back to Up: the balloon house rising between brick buildings, with a thin white outline of the Arc logo drawn over it.
shot_notes.38: The logo holds over the house as it climbs. The film's two homes, the Pixar house and the browser, share one frame.
shot_notes.39: 'Arc for iPhone' on black in the same serif. The product's name is the last thing written and the only time it appears.
shot_notes.40: The title holds to the end with the song still playing.

motion_intro: The film has almost no movement of its own. Nearly every moving thing is borrowed: people packing, running, pushing a van, a house on balloons. What the editors control is the cut and the type. Shots average about 1.3 seconds and get shorter through the packing montage, the white serif sentence either holds still across cuts or stands alone on black, and the few designed moves are the app's own: a smiley that blinks, spaces swiped sideways, an icon flickering through its variants, and a logo outline laid over the last shot. The sequences below follow those cuts and the type across them.

motion.title: One word holds while the clips change under it
motion.text: 'Home' dissolves on at about 1.3 over a flash-lit laptop on a messy desk and is solid by 1.5. At 2.34 a hard cut drops to near black, a face lit by a laptop, and the word does not move or change size: it sits exactly where it was. It holds until 3.45, then cuts away with the shot to a sleeping figure. Because the text ignores the cut, the two clips read as examples of one word rather than as a story.

motion.title: 'What if', and the music comes in
motion.text: A woman lifts a laptop over her head in a pale room ('What's out there?' at 5.5), a hand gropes across a dark table from 6.42, and at 7.17 a man in black and white looks around an empty room. 'What' appears on him at about 7.25 and 'if' joins it at 7.5. As 'Where's my phone?' is heard, the music stem jumps about 15 dB, from around -28 to -13 dB, at 7.75, and at 7.92 a hard cut lands on a teal backpack in color with hands grabbing it. Monochrome and quiet give way to color and full volume on the same beat the question is asked.

motion.title: The caption rides a blur, then lands on the snail
motion.text: 'you could bring home with you' comes on with a hard cut at 9.93 to a drawer being emptied, a smear of white sleeve and dark clothes. The line sits mid-frame through the blur and stays on across the cut at 11.51 to a snail crawling over gravel, then leaves at about 12.0 so the snail has a second alone. The caption ends on the one image that says it without words.

motion.title: Packing, then leaving, a little faster each time
motion.text: Mr. Bean stuffs a suitcase (12.76, letterboxed 4:3), someone hurries down a hallway (13.72), a tent goes up in the desert (14.81), a family rushes down a staircase (15.64), luggage is shoved into a convertible (16.23), the Little Miss Sunshine family pushes its van (16.81) and leaps aboard (17.56), and a bus piled with bags drives at camera (18.23). Shots fall from about a second to 0.58 s and then lengthen again for the bus. The motion inside each clip is all forward and away, so the sequence moves from rooms out onto roads without any designed move.

motion.title: Watching the house go by
motion.text: At 3.84 s this Up shot is the longest in the film. The balloon house drifts across a window from top left, seen mostly as a reflection behind a mother and her children, while a father steps in from the right at about 20.8. By 22.4 the family has turned to each other, wide-eyed. The film slows here, on people watching a home travel, just as the song's vocal begins at about 19.5.

motion.title: 'You can', 'Hi there', 'Let's go', run
motion.text: 'You can' sits alone on black from 23.15 to 24.07, a cyclist crosses a black-and-white street to 24.98, and the first product frame is Arc's onboarding screen: a white smiley and 'Hi there' on a shifting purple gradient. The smiley blinks at about 25.46, eyes closing to dots for a single frame. At 26.05 it cuts to the app's 'Let's go' button, and at 26.61 to Jules and Jim racing across a footbridge. The app's own onboarding copy is cut as if it were a line in the film, and old footage answers it.

motion.title: Spaces swiped sideways, a list rearranged
motion.text: The phone screen is shown small and unframed, floating in the middle of black with no device around it. The purple 'Browser co' space sits from 27.36, slides left at about 28.3 to reveal the pink 'Crafting' space, which holds until a black card interrupts at 28.95. At 29.86 'Crafting' returns and slides off at about 30.2 to the yellow 'Home' space. From 30.6 the Home list scrolls up and at about 31.3 'Murakami's vinyl collection' is dragged up into the list. Each space has its own color, so a swipe reads as a change of room.

motion.title: The end of the sentence lifts off
motion.text: 'is now in your pocket' arrives on black at 31.86 and stays put through two cuts: at 32.62 to a black-and-white hot-air balloon shot from beneath, its basket swinging, and at 33.62 to a balloon drifting away beyond a tree. The type is the same size and position on black and on footage, and the images under it rise, so the line about being portable ends on things floating away.

motion.title: The app icon flickers through its variants
motion.text: A white iPhone home screen with only a search pill and three icons: Spotify, Arc and Messages. From 34.76 Arc's icon changes every one or two frames at 24 fps: the classic red and blue mark, a dark 'Arc' badge, a purple tile, a pastel candy version, a pretzel, a blurred dark blue one, and round again, a dozen or so swaps in 2.6 seconds. The neighbours never move. It shows a small feature (alternate app icons) and also says, without a word, that the app is now on your phone among the apps you already use.

motion.title: The logo drawn over the flying house
motion.text: At 37.33 the film cuts back to Up, now looking up a street between brick buildings at the balloon house rising. A thin white outline of the Arc logo sits over the house, still, while the house climbs past it. It holds for 1.5 seconds before 'Arc for iPhone' appears on black at 38.87. The house that stood for the idea and the mark that stands for the product share one frame.

lede: A forty-one second launch spot for Arc's iPhone app that is mostly not about the app. It is a montage of borrowed film clips (people alone with laptops at night, a snail, Mr. Bean packing, the Little Miss Sunshine van, the flying house from Up, the footbridge race from Jules and Jim) under one sentence spread across nine seconds of black cards and captions: 'Home. What if you could bring home with you? You can. Your home on the internet is now in your pocket.' The product appears for about seven seconds, as a smiley, a few lists and an icon.

What is worth learning is how far an idea can be carried by other people's pictures. Arc had already called itself a home on the internet, and 'home' is the only idea the film develops: first as screens people live in, then as something you pack and take with you. The clips do the emotional work, the sentence does the arguing, and the app's own words ('Hi there', 'Let's go', a space named Home) are cut in as if they were lines in the film.

aspects.title: One word, turned over twice
paragraphs: The whole film is built on 'home'. It opens by showing the internet as the place people already live: a laptop between a pizza slice and a plastic bag, faces lit blue in dark rooms, someone asleep at the desk. 'Home' over those shots is half joke and half true, and it borrows the idea Arc had already used for itself on the desktop.

Then the word turns. 'What if you could bring home with you' changes home from a place you are stuck in to something you can carry, and the clips change with it: a snail, suitcases, a tent, a van, a bus with luggage on the roof, and finally a house lifted by balloons. By the time the sentence resumes with 'Your home on the internet is now in your pocket', the viewer has already seen a dozen ways to take a home along, and the app only has to be the last one.

The answer is very short. 'You can' sits on black for under a second, and the product follows straight away with its own greeting. The film spends twenty-three seconds on the question and wish, and about seven on the app.

moments.text: 'Home' over a laptop on a messy desk.
'What if', on a man looking around an empty room.
The snail: a home on its back.
'You can', alone on black.

aspects.title: A borrowed montage with a house of its own
paragraphs: Almost every shot comes from somewhere else: a sitcom, an indie road movie, Pixar, the French New Wave, footage of strangers. They are not regraded to match. Black-and-white clips stay black and white, a 4:3 Mr. Bean shot keeps its black bars, and the bicycle shot is pillarboxed. The mix of formats is part of the look, closer to a fan supercut or a moodboard than to an ad shoot, and it suits a product whose users collect things from all over the web.

The cutting follows the idea, not the beat. The audio check finds 7 of 30 cuts within 70 ms of the music's beat, about what chance would give. Instead the shots get shorter as the packing speeds up (down to 0.58 s around 15.6 to 16.8) and then the film stops on the Up window for 3.8 seconds, its longest shot, so the flying house gets time to land.

Up is used twice, and that is the structural trick. The first time, the house passes a window and a family stares. The second time, at the end, it rises between buildings with the Arc logo drawn over it. The borrowed image that carried the idea comes back carrying the brand.

aspects.title: A sentence spread across the cuts
paragraphs: There is no narrator. The script is one sentence, broken into six pieces and written in a plain white serif: 'Home', 'What if', 'you could bring home with you', 'You can', 'Your home on the internet', 'is now in your pocket', then 'Arc for iPhone'. Each piece is either alone on black or laid across footage like a subtitle, and when it is on footage it usually holds through a cut, so the words feel steadier than the pictures.
The serif matters. It reads like a film title or a book, not like app marketing, and it sets the borrowed clips up as cinema. The only sans serif type in the film belongs to the app's own screens.

Two spoken lines come from the clips, 'What's out there?' and 'Where's my phone?', and both happen to be the question the film is asking. Later the app speaks for itself: its onboarding says 'Hi there' and 'Let's go', and the edit treats those as lines of dialogue, cutting from 'Let's go' straight to three friends running.

moments.text: 'Home' holds while the clip under it changes.
The caption sits across a blur, like a subtitle.
The app's 'Let's go', used as a line.
Jules and Jim answer it by running.

aspects.title: Seven seconds of product, all of it personal
paragraphs: The app gets three short passages: the onboarding greeting, a swipe through three spaces, and the home screen icon. None of them explains a feature. The screens are shown small and unframed on black, without a phone around them, so they read as one more image in the montage rather than as a demo.

What they show is chosen to fit the theme. The spaces have their own colors and human names (Browser co, Crafting, Home), and the items in them are specific and a little private: 'Crochet Stitches', 'Starting a Sashiko', 'Home buys', 'June trip', 'Murakami's vinyl collection'. The last space is literally called Home. A viewer sees someone's interests, not a tab manager.

The icon passage does two jobs at once. Arc's icon flickers through its alternate designs between Spotify and Messages, which shows off a small feature and also places Arc on the home screen among the apps people already keep there.

aspects.title: Quiet question, loud answer
paragraphs: The music is the only designed sound, and it has one big move. For the first seven and a half seconds it sits around -28 dB under the lonely-laptop clips and the first spoken line. At 7.75, as 'Where's my phone?' is heard and just before the cut to the teal backpack, the music stem jumps about 15 dB and stays loud for the rest of the film. The same moment is the switch from black and white to color. The question is asked quietly and the packing starts at full volume.

A sung vocal enters at about 19.5, as the Up shot begins. Its words are not clear enough to transcribe, but its breaths are visible in the voice track, and the black title cards sit near them: the vocal drops out from about 23.0 to 24.3, almost exactly the second 'You can' is on screen, and there are similar gaps around 28.0 to 29.0 and 32.3 to 33.5, close to the next two cards. The cards are placed where the singer leaves room.

moments.text: Quiet music under 'What's out there?'.
The music jumps to full level on the cut to color.
The song's vocal comes in with Up.
'You can' in a pause in the vocal.

patterns.name: Develop one word, not a feature list
patterns.text: Pick the word your brand already owns (here 'home') and spend the film turning it over: first what it means now, then what it could mean. The product only needs to be the last example.

patterns.name: Let found footage carry the feeling
patterns.text: Clips everyone half-remembers bring their own emotion. Choose them for one shared action (packing, leaving, floating) and keep their original formats instead of cropping them to match.

patterns.name: Hold the words still across cuts
patterns.text: Let a caption stay in place while the shots change beneath it. The words become the steady thread and the clips become examples of them.

patterns.name: Cut the product's own copy in as dialogue
patterns.text: Use the interface's real words ('Hi there', 'Let's go') as lines, and answer them with footage, so the app feels like a character instead of a demo.

patterns.name: Make the demo content personal
patterns.text: Fill the screens with specific, human item names and a space called Home. Viewers read a person's interests, which carries the warmth the montage built.

patterns.name: Bring the borrowed image back with your mark on it
patterns.text: Reuse the clip that best stood for the idea as the end card, with the logo laid over it, so the metaphor and the brand meet in one frame.

patterns.name: Hit the music at the turn
patterns.text: Keep the score low under the setup and let it jump at the exact moment the film turns from problem to wish, together with a change in the picture.

craft.absent: There is no narrator, no on-camera person from the company, no feature explanation and almost no original footage. Its cuts are not timed to the beat, and the clips are not color-matched. Study it for building a launch film around one word and other people's pictures.
